module_title: Foundation Model Customization, Evaluation and Bedrock Applications
review_basis: Visually inspected original numbered WebP slides 25 through 28 individually, including CloudWatch metric namespaces, pricing modes, model-improvement comparison and cost-optimization decisions; concise visual-first narration reviewed.

scenes.title: Observe Amazon Bedrock with CloudWatch
scenes.narration: This slide separates operational metrics from optional request logging. Start at the left: applications send requests to Amazon Bedrock, and Bedrock publishes supported metrics to Amazon CloudWatch. In the center dashboard, you can see invocation count, latency, errors and throttling. Invocation count tells us how often the model is called; latency measures response time; throttling indicates requests being limited. The green Guardrails metric, InvocationsIntervened, counts supported guardrail interventions. Below the dashboard, notice the namespaces AWS slash Bedrock for runtime metrics and AWS slash Bedrock slash Guardrails for guardrail metrics. Teams can create alarms for error spikes or slower responses. The separate pink panel on the right is optional invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3 for supported calls. It is not the same as metrics and is not enabled by default. Logs may contain sensitive prompts or responses, so control access, retention and permissions carefully. Use metrics for operational health; enable detailed logging only when its diagnostic value justifies the privacy risk.

scenes.title: Amazon Bedrock pricing: identify the cost drivers
scenes.narration: This slide compares four Bedrock billing patterns. On-demand usage on the left charges according to consumption, such as input and output text tokens, embedding input or image generation, depending on the selected model. A token is a small unit of text processed or produced by the model. More output generally means more billed output tokens. The next panel shows batch inference: eligible offline workloads process files asynchronously and store results in Amazon S3. Think of generating summaries overnight rather than waiting for each request interactively. Third, provisioned capacity reserves throughput for supported models, useful when demand is steady and predictable, but it creates a capacity commitment. Fourth, customizing a model can introduce training and deployed-model costs in addition to application usage. Look at the examples across the bottom: interactive chat fits on-demand, overnight document summaries may fit batch, and stable high traffic may justify provisioned capacity. There is no single universal Bedrock price. Compare the chosen model, AWS Region, workload size and current pricing before selecting an option.

scenes.title: Choose a model-improvement technique by need and effort
scenes.narration: This slide offers a decision ladder for improving model behavior. Start at the left with prompting: instructions, context and examples guide a model without changing its weights. Next is RAG, which retrieves external facts and adds them to a prompt, also without updating weights. Instruction fine-tuning is different: labeled input-output examples update a supported model's weights to teach consistent behavior or format. Continued pre-training updates weights using a much larger collection of domain text, helping the model adapt to specialized language. On the far right, training from scratch builds a model from the beginning and usually requires the greatest data and engineering effort. The arrow at the bottom is a general effort guideline, not a guaranteed price ranking for every workload. Use the decision cards below it: for a response style, start with a better prompt; for frequently changing company facts, choose RAG; for specialized terminology or stable task behavior, evaluate supported customization. The key distinction is whether you need fresh source information or a change in the model's learned behavior. Always compare performance and total cost before committing.

scenes.title: Reduce Bedrock cost while preserving quality
scenes.narration: The goal here is to lower Bedrock cost without damaging answer quality. Follow the numbered steps. First measure input tokens, output tokens and request counts, as shown in the usage dashboard. Second, try a smaller model and keep it only if it passes your quality checks; the green and yellow decision boxes illustrate that choice. Third, remove unnecessary prompt context and cap outputs where appropriate, rather than generating long replies by default. Fourth, use caching for repeated or similar requests when the result can safely be reused. Fifth, consider batch processing for eligible offline work instead of many individual real-time requests. Sixth, compare on-demand with provisioned throughput: reserved capacity suits predictable demand but is not automatically cheaper. The bottom strip adds an important clarification. Sampling settings such as temperature change response behavior; they do not directly set the per-token price. However, generating more tokens can still increase the bill. Reevaluate costs alongside factual quality, response time and reliability, rather than optimizing only for the cheapest model.
